paragraphs.source_en: The master went on thinking: “If I go on comparing myself only with madmen like this, counting up nothing but the points of resemblance, I shall never be able to escape the domain of madness. Perhaps my method is wrong. It is because I have taken madmen as my standard and forcibly drawn myself toward them in my interpretation that I have reached this conclusion. If I took healthy people as the standard and considered myself beside them, I might perhaps arrive at the opposite result. In that case, let me begin with those close at hand. First, what about Meitei’s uncle, who came here today in a frock coat? Where on earth is one to place his mind? That old gentleman is rather unreliable even as a standard of normality. Second, what about Kangetsu? He goes to work carrying his lunch and spends morning till night doing nothing but polishing balls. No, no, he too must be crossed off. Then who is third? Meitei? That fellow regards fooling about as his divine calling; he is without doubt a cheerful sort of madman. Then fourth? Kaneda’s wife. Her venomous disposition is utterly beyond common sense; she is pure and simple a neurotic case. Fifth comes Kaneda himself. I have never met Kaneda, but seeing how reverently he props up that wife of his, obeying her every word and living in such conjugal harmony, one may well regard him as an extraordinary man; and since extraordinary is another name for mad, he too may be placed among that class. Who comes next? There are more, more indeed: the gentlemen of Rakunkan. In age they are still mere fledglings, yet in frenzy they may fairly be called splendid champions mighty enough to sweep an age away. Counting them up one by one like this, most of them seem to be of the same breed as madmen. That rather puts my mind at ease. Perhaps society itself is nothing but a gathering of madmen: madmen assembling together, jostling, grappling, snarling, abusing, and plundering one another, while the whole mass, as a body, splits apart like cells and swells up, swells up and splits apart again, continuing so from day to day. That may be what is called society. It may well be that anyone among them who understands a little reason and can distinguish right from wrong becomes a nuisance, so they invented the madhouse, shut him up there, and made sure he could never come out again. Looked at in that way, those who are said to be confined in madhouses are ordinary people, while those raging outside the madhouse are the madmen. So long as a madman is alone, he will be treated as a madman to the end; but once madmen form a group and gain power, perhaps they become sound people. There are more than a few cases in which a great madman abuses the power of money and authority, sets many little madmen to acts of violence, and is praised by people as a fine fellow. What in the world is all this? I no longer understand it.”

paragraphs.source_zh: 主人接着又想：“像这样一味把自己和疯子比较，专去寻找类似之点，那么，无论如何也难从疯子的领域里摆脱出来。这可能是我的方法不对头。是以疯子为基准，把自己往上硬凑加以解释的，所以才得出这样的结论。假如以正常人为标准，将自己和他们放在一起来考虑的话，也许会得出相反的结果。既然这样，就让我先从身边的人开始。第一个，今天来家的那位身穿大礼服的迷亭的伯父怎么样？你自己的心是往哪儿放呀？那老头儿，连做正常人的标准也有些靠不住。第二，寒月怎么样？带着饭盒去上班，从早到晚，只是一味地磨圆球，不成，不成，也得把他抹掉。那么第三呢？迷亭？那家伙把胡开玩笑当成他的天职，无疑是个阳性的疯子。那么第四呢？金田的老婆。她那恶毒的心性，完全超乎常识，纯粹是个神经病。第五就轮到金田啦，我虽然没有和金田见过面，但看他那种恭恭敬敬地把老婆捧着，言听计从、琴瑟调和的样子，应该把他看成是个非凡的人，非凡就是疯子的别名，所以也可以将他归入疯子一类。再往下呢？还有，还有，还有落云馆的各位君子哪。从年龄说，虽然还是些黄口孺子，但在狂躁这点上，满可以说是风靡一世的、超凡的豪强。这样一个一个地数起来看，大都是疯子的同类。这样，倒让我放心啦。说不定，也许社会就是疯子的集合体，疯子聚在一起，互相争斗，互相仇视，互相谩骂，互相争夺，而他的整体作为一个集团，像细胞那样忽而散裂忽而又膨大起来，忽而膨大忽而又散裂开来，一天天这样继续下去。这可能就是所谓的社会吧。很可能在其中有个多少懂点道理、明辨是非的人，反而会变得碍眼，于是才造了疯人院，把他圈到里边去让他再也无法出来的吧。这样看来所谓幽闭在疯人院里的人倒是普通人，而在疯人院外边闹腾的人却是疯子。疯子在他是单个人的时候，会始终被人们当做疯子，但是成为一个团体，有了势力，说不定就成了健全人呢。大疯子滥用他的金钱力量和威力，指使那些小疯子胡作非为，人们反而称赞大疯子是个了不起的人物，这样的事例多得很。这到底是怎么回事呀？我也弄不明白。”

paragraphs.source_en: The foregoing is a faithful account of the workings of the master’s mind as he sank into meditation that night beneath his lonely lamp. The opacity of his brain is strikingly apparent in this matter as well. Though he wears a Kaiser Wilhelm II moustache, he is such a muddlehead that he cannot even distinguish a lunatic from an ordinary man. Nor is that all: after taking the trouble to pose this problem to himself and appeal to his own reason, he reached no conclusion whatsoever and simply stopped thinking. In everything, he is a man utterly lacking the capacity to think matters through. The fact that his conclusions are vague and elusive, as hard to grasp as the smoke of an Asahi cigarette bursting from his nostrils, should be remembered forever as the sole distinguishing feature of his arguments.

paragraphs.source_zh: 以上，我如实地叙述了主人当天夜里在茕茕孤灯之下进行沉思默想时的心理活动。他的头脑不透明的特点，也充分显示在这个问题上。别看他蓄着德皇威廉二世式的八字胡，但却是个连狂人与平常人都辨别不出的糊涂虫。还不只是如此，他好不容易地给自己提出问题，诉之于自己的理性，结果却未能得出任何结论，就不再去想了。不管什么事他都是个完全缺乏思考力的人。他的结论就像从他鼻孔喷出来的朝日牌香烟的烟雾一样，茫漠缥缈，难以捉摸，这是他所发议论的唯一特色，应该永远记住。
